entities.name: Conrad of Gelnhausen
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Conrad of Gelnhausen (died April 13, 1390), a pivotal German theologian and master of canon law, emerged as one of the foundational intellectual architects of the conciliar movement in the late fourteenth century. His radical proposals, articulated during the tumultuous Western Schism (1378-1417), directly challenged papal absolutism, advocating for the supremacy of a general council over the authority of a single pontiff. Operating primarily from universities in Paris and Heidelberg, Conrad's writings provided a crucial theoretical framework for reformers seeking to heal the schism and restructure the governance of the Catholic Church, thereby influencing subsequent ecclesiastical reforms and political thought across Europe.

Educated at the University of Paris, where he earned a doctorate in theology, Conrad's academic career laid the groundwork for his later activism. His most influential treatise, the *Epistola concordiae* (Letter on Concord), written around 1380, boldly asserted that a general council had the authority to judge and even depose a pope, particularly in cases of schism or heresy. This work, along with his *De modo unionis et reformationis ecclesiae* (On the Method of Uniting and Reforming the Church), argued that the Church's ultimate authority resided in the community of the faithful, represented by a council, rather than solely in the pope. These arguments were revolutionary, providing a legitimate theological basis for convening a council to resolve the unprecedented crisis of two, and later three, rival popes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Conrad of Gelnhausen's intellectual contributions provided critical theological and legal justification for the conciliar movement, directly influencing the resolution of the Western Schism and shaping debates on church governance for centuries. His work represents a significant challenge to papal absolutism within late medieval Christendom.
